item.title: [arXiv-SE 2026] The Hidden Costs of Forgetting: A Study of Trajectory Deletion in Software Engineering Agents
item.description: arXiv:2610.35496v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Software engineering agents resend their entire trajectory to an LLM at every turn, motivating online trajectory reduction. Prior work shows that randomly deleting 75% of tokens in old turns may preserve agent effectiveness, but it remains unclear why, how agents compensate for missing content, and whether it actually reduces costs. This paper presents an empirical study of 42 trajectory-reduction configurations, focusing on effectiveness, agent behavior, and cost. We systematically explore deleting content from old turns by varying the scope, granularity, amount, and timing of deletion across 9,400 runs with two state-of-the-art agents on SWE-bench Verified. We find deleting large amounts of trajectory content (e.g., up to 100% of reasoning text) can preserve overall effectiveness. Importantly, such deletion must be applied with a delay, as immediate deletion tends to significantly degrade effectiveness. Agents often compensate for deleted content by re-fetching it, increasing both the number of turns taken and the input/output tokens. Whether trajectory reduction reduces costs depends on the pricing model: Under a flat pricing model, estimated costs fall in 26 of 42 evaluations. Surprisingly, under a caching-aware pricing model, zero evaluations yield lower costs, since reducing the trajectory breaks the cached prefix billed at a lower rate. Our findings have three implications: First, token counts alone are misleading; trajectory reduction techniques must consider overall costs under a realistic pricing model. Second, analyzing trajectories is crucial to understand agent behavior, as end-to-end effectiveness hides differences such as excessive re-fetching. Finally, these results highlight the need for future work on memory management to reduce costs without sacrificing effectiveness.
item.author: cs.SE updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-SE 2026] Ranking Function Generation with LLMs for Termination
item.description: arXiv:2610.35523v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ranking functions are a fundamental technique for proving loop termination, but constructing them manually is challenging and requires substantial expertise. We propose RAINFALL, a neuro-symbolic framework which follows the generate-verify-refine paradigm and tightly integrates LLMs with symbolic verification. RAINFALL formulates ranking function synthesis as a code-completion task by inserting placeholders into the input program and constraining the LLM to fill four predefined slots for each loop. The completed program is then checked by a symbolic verifier. If verification succeeds, a valid ranking function is obtained; otherwise, the verifier's diagnostics are translated into natural-language feedback that guides iterative refinement of the LLM's output. We evaluate RAINFALL on two public benchmark suites comprising 358 terminating C programs. Using MiniMax V2.7, RAINFALL synthesizes verifiable ranking functions for 323 programs (90.22%), outperforming all promising baselines. In particular, it solves 12 more programs than PROTON 2.1, the best-performing baseline and winner of the SV-COMP 2026 Termination category. Furthermore, combining RAINFALL with PROTON 2.1 increases the success rate to 96.65% (346/358 programs). We also conduct ablation study confirming individual contributions of placeholder contracts, few-shot examples, symbolic verification, and diagnostic information feedback. Experiments across LLMs further confirm the effectiveness of RAINFALL. Our results suggest a generic, sound framework for ranking-function synthesis and, beyond termination, LLM-assisted synthesis of formally checkable liveness certificates, both of which represent new directions of software engineering research.
item.author: cs.SE updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-SE 2026] SWE-Ladder: Learning to Localize, Reproduce, and Patch via Progressive Privileged Self-Distillation
item.description: arXiv:2610.33667v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Resolving a repository-level issue typically requires a software-engineering (SWE) agent to localize the faulty code, reproduce the failure, and patch the code. Reinforcement learning trains such agents from a single test result on the final patch, while on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) adds token-level supervision from a teacher with privileged evidence, exposing the full reference patch at every step. Neither provides stage-specific guidance for localization or reproduction. We propose SWE-Ladder, which turns the verified repair of each training instance into stage-specific evidence: the changed files and lines for localization, the fail-to-pass tests for reproduction, and the diff for patching. A rule-based router assigns each step of an end-to-end rollout to a stage based on its tool call, a frozen teacher sees only the matching evidence, and the stages are distilled in repair order while GRPO optimizes the full trajectory. With Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 on SWE-bench Verified under the R2E-Gym scaffold, SWE-Ladder improves pass@1 from 9.6% to 16.4%, compared with 10.4% for GRPO and 12.4% for OPSD with the full patch. Under the OpenHands scaffold, it improves pass@1 from 13.0% to 17.6%. Reversing the stage order under R2E-Gym reduces pass@1 to 11.4%.
item.author: cs.SE updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-SE 2026] GPU-Accelerated Belief Propagation for Program Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2509.22337v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Belief Propagation (BP) is a widely used approximate inference algorithm in probabilistic graphical models (PGMs), but is computationally expensive when applied to large-scale program analysis. Existing GPU-based approaches are unable to support flexible update strategies and have yet to integrate logical constraints with GPU acceleration, leading to challenges in both generality and efficiency. We present FastLBP, a GPU-accelerated BP framework for program analysis. We propose a unified representation for specifying flexible update strategies required in program analysis, along with a dependency analysis algorithm to enable parallel execution. Furthermore, we implement BP with local structures on GPUs by assigning individual threads to message computations and utilizing a memory-efficient representation. Experiments on SmartFL and BINGO show that FastLBP achieves average speedups of $17.42\times$ and $2.82\times$ over CPU-based approaches on SmartFL and BINGO, respectively, and $6.14\times$ over GPU-based approach on SmartFL, while preserving accuracy. Moreover, FastLBP supports update strategies that existing GPU-based approaches cannot support, demonstrating its improved generality for real-world program analysis.
item.author: cs.SE updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-SE 2026] EviACT: An Evidence-to-Action Framework for Agentic Program Repair
item.description: arXiv:2605.27238v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: LLM-based agents have moved automated program repair (APR) from fixed-context patch generation to interactive repository-level repair. However, existing agentic APR systems still struggle to use execution evidence to guide localization, patch generation, and validation. We propose EviACT (Evidence-to-Action), an agentic APR framework that coordinates three evidence-driven guardrails across repair stages. The retrieval scaffold grounds repair context, the compile gate filters invalid edits, and the test-driven gate checks target-test recovery before full regression. Across four benchmarks, EviACT improves resolve rate over the strongest reported comparable baselines by 1.6-6.0 percentage points and shows 70.1-88.6% lower reported per-bug API cost where baseline costs are available. Ablations and diagnostics suggest that these gains are associated with the coordinated evidence-to-action chain, making agentic APR more effective and efficient.
item.author: cs.SE updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-SE 2026] Enhancing Software Engineering Through Closed-Loop Memory Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2606.05646v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have enabled powerful software engineering (SE) agents capable of navigating complex codebases and resolving real-world issues. However, these agents remain fundamentally episodic: they fail to retain, refine, and reuse experiences across tasks, repeatedly reconstructing context from scratch and reproducing similar mistakes. Even with memory support, they offer no remedy for the absence of a principled, task-agnostic \textit{memory utility}, making them difficult to evaluate rigorously or generalize across agents and settings. To tackle these limitations, we introduce MemOp, a closed-loop framework for memory augmentation in SE agents. MemOp grounds memory utility in \textit{validated downstream impact}, establishing utility as both a task-agnostic \textbf{evaluation benchmark} and an annotation-free \textbf{optimization signal}. Evaluating MemOp across four benchmarks, three programming languages, and two SE agents, under complementary \textit{single-episode} and \textit{cross-episode} memory augmentation, results demonstrate the \textbf{effectiveness} of MemOp, achieving absolute gains of up to $\uparrow5.25\%$ in success rate and $\uparrow4.63\%$ in resolve efficiency, while notably reducing deployment cost by $\geq10.33\%$. MemOp further exhibits \textbf{generalizability} across SE agents, memory backbones, and optimization algorithms, together with \textbf{transferability} of MemOp-trained memory model to unseen programming languages and SE activities. Our project page: https://xhguo7.github.io/MemOp/.
item.author: cs.SE updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-SE 2026] Terminus-4B: Can a Smaller Model Replace Frontier LLMs at Agentic Execution Tasks?
item.description: arXiv:2605.03195v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Modern coding agents increasingly delegate specialized subtasks to subagents, which are smaller, focused agentic loops that handle narrow responsibilities like search, debugging or terminal execution. This architectural pattern keeps the main agent's context window clean by isolating verbose outputs (e.g. build logs, test results, etc.) within the subagent context. Typically when agents employ subagents for such tasks, they use frontier models as these subagents. In this paper, we investigate whether a finetuned small language model (SLM) can achieve comparable performance to frontier models in the task of agentic terminal execution. We present Terminus-4B, which is a post-trained Qwen3-4B model via Supervised Finetuning (SFT) and Reinforcement Learning (RL) using rubric-based LLM-as-judge reward, specifically for this task. In our extensive evaluation spanning various frontier models, training ablations and main agent configurations, we find that Terminus-4B is able to reduce the token usage of the main agent by up to ~30% compared to the No Subagent baseline with no impact to agent performance on benchmarks like SWE-Bench Pro and our internal SWE-Bench C# benchmark, which tends to be heavy in verbose execution tasks. Furthermore, Terminus-4B improves key metrics showing the main agent relying on the outputs of the subagent and doing fewer terminal execution tasks by itself. We see that our model not only closes the gap between the Vanilla Qwen model and frontier models like Claude Sonnet / Opus / GPT-5.3-Codex, but often even exceeds their performance.
item.author: cs.SE updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-PL 2026] PastaLean: Deterministic transpilation from Python to Lean for Verification
item.description: arXiv:2610.34205v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present PastaLean, an extensible system for deterministic translation from Python to Lean via the Abstract Syntax Tree of Python. This allows for verification of Python code, especially auxiliary code used by AI. Every program is translated into a provable twin written in the form Lean's verification tooling can reason about, and a runnable twin that gives a fast and correct computation support. We also introduce our Type Inference engine TypeInfer which provides static typing support for untyped Python code. Our tool provides coverage of more than 92\% for LeetCode and HumanEval\textsuperscript{+} and more than 98\% for LiveCodeBench ground truth Python files. Further, at least 97\% of each dataset's (numerical) test cases pass, with 100\% on HumanEval\textsuperscript{+} and LiveCodeBench. The TypeInfer engine is the best-scoring tool on the TypeEvalPy static leaderboard, and on a repository-level TypyBench benchmark it scores above every competing repository-level inference tool.
item.author: cs.PL updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-CL 2026] MechAlign: Evaluating Semantic Alignment at the Project Level in Mathematical Formalization
item.description: arXiv:2610.35269v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Lean verifies that a formal proof establishes its stated proposition under declared assumptions, but does not check whether that proposition faithfully expresses the mathematical claim in a manuscript. Assessing this correspondence requires interpreting the main theorem through its project dependencies, which may be scattered throughout a large development. We introduce MechAlign, a framework for project-level semantic alignment review that combines formal dependency extraction with LLM-based assessment. Its extraction tool, LeanTrace, constructs a statement dependency graph from elaborated declarations, retaining definition bodies and structure constraints while excluding proof bodies and stopping at an explicit library boundary. The reviewer uses this context to investigate alignment and report discrepancies with localized evidence. We conduct a preliminary review of 201 main results from 173 OpenAI Math projects, using supplied informal descriptions and available paper context. A hyperbolic-group case illustrates how dependency inspection localizes a missing dimensional constraint relative to the manuscript, consistent with the upstream declaration of formalization scope. We also construct LeanReviewBench, comprising 501 fixed claim-statement-context triples from OpenAI Math, Fermat's Last Theorem, and Kakeya, with description provenance recorded. The resource supports controlled comparisons of more project-level semantic alignment evaluations.
item.author: cs.CL updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-CL 2026] Hierarchical Skill Evolution for Coding Agent
item.description: arXiv:2610.35616v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Skills provide agents with reusable experience to guide future decisions without modifying the underlying model. However, coding trajectories are often entangled with task- and repository-specific contexts, making it challenging to distill procedural skills that generalize across diverse coding environments. To address this challenge, we present Hierarchical Skill Evolution (HSE), which progressively distills procedural knowledge from coding trajectories through hierarchical evidence aggregation. HSE first extracts task-level evidence from individual trajectories, then aggregates recurring evidence within the same repository to form repository-specific skill candidates, and finally consolidates consistent patterns across repositories into transferable skills across repositories. The evolution is driven by an external writer-evaluator loop that generates and assesses skills while keeping the underlying coding model frozen. The loop externally updates the writer and evaluator policies to improve subsequent skill generation and assessment. This hierarchy progressively filters task-specific details while preserving procedures that generalize across diverse coding environments. Successful trajectories yield reusable guidance for future tasks, while failed trajectories reveal recurring failure modes that guide avoidance and recovery. We evaluate HSE on SWE-bench Verified and DeepSWE, using GLM-5.2 across Pi and Claude Code harnesses and GPT-5.5 and Opus 4.8 with Pi. Across both benchmarks, 10 skills evolved solely from SWE-Gym improve coding performance across all evaluated settings, demonstrating transfer across benchmarks, coding models, and agent harnesses. We further evolve the skill library from target-benchmark trajectories without verifier feedback, relying solely on the learned evaluator for candidate assessment and achieving additional gains through benchmark-tailored skills.
item.author: cs.CL updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-CL 2026] LLMs Can Tackle High Energy Theoretical Physics, yet Gaps Remain: Part I, Quantum Field Theory
item.description: arXiv:2610.33134v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Beyond math and code, Large language models (LLMs) are beginning to tackle problems that have traditionally required substantial training for theoretical physicists, but it remains unclear how far this capability extends and where it might break. As a first step toward pushing LLMs in high-energy theoretical physics, we introduce QFT-Bench, a benchmark of 75 graduate- to research-level problems requiring extensive reasoning and derivation across core Quantum Field Theory (QFT) subareas. Each question has a well-defined target and closed-form reference answer. Evaluation combines symbolic verification with LLM-based judge. Across 39 proprietary and open-source models, frontier models already demonstrate substantial capabilities on nontrivial QFT calculations, with the strongest models exceeding 95% accuracy. At the same time, clear gaps remain. Even strong models still make errors in calculations, conventions, and instruction following, while weaker models often fail at the level of physical concepts or derivations. We further monitor models' CoTs and show that current models exhibit nontrivial reasoning unfaithfulness, i.e., they could reach correct answers but the reasoning itself does not justify and logically support them. These results provide a quantitative assessment of current LLM capabilities in QFT and a first step toward broader evaluation in high-energy theoretical physics.
item.author: cs.CL updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-CR 2026] SEMPRE: Semantic-Aware Protocol Reverse Engineering via Consistency-Driven Joint Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2610.31844v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Protocol reverse engineering (PRE) is essential for understanding undocumented or proprietary communication formats, enabling security-critical tasks such as vulnerability discovery, malware C2 analysis, and IDS signature generation. However, existing PRE techniques rely on brittle hand-written rules, under-model contextual dependencies among neighboring fields, and often fail on messages with nested sub-protocols. We present SEMPRE, a fully automated PRE framework that replaces ad-hoc heuristics with recursive LLM reasoning grounded in fine-grained dynamic program analysis. SEMPRE uses taint-flow and loop traces to guide an LLM-driven tree-of-thought search that slices messages into fields while detecting nested sub-payloads, producing a hierarchical layout. It then infers each field's type and role and iteratively refines boundaries by freezing high-confidence segments and re-running detection under semantic constraints, yielding an EM-style procedure that monotonically improves structure and semantics until convergence. Evaluated on a broad corpus of mainstream protocols against six state-of-the-art (vs. <0.4 for all baselines) and 0.72 for semantic inference (vs. 0.13 for BinPRE). Ablations confirm the contribution of each component, and a case study on a prolific real-world botnet demonstrates practical utility.
item.author: cs.CR updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-CR 2026] EVSEFuzz : A Tool for Automated Testing of Protocol Implementations
item.description: arXiv:2610.32902v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rapid adoption and development of electric vehicle (EV) networks has required the expansive deployment of EV charging infrastructure (EVCI) which relies on communication protocols such as the open charge point protocol (OCPP) to coordinate data transfer between charging network operators and the EV supply equipment. In this paper, we present EVSEFuzz, a tool for automatically building fuzzers to test the security of protocol implementations. To achieve this we make a novel use of Python datatype validation packages and tools to ``understand'' datatypes and message structures and generate both compliant and non-compliant messages. To date, EVSEFuzz has been tested successfully with several open and closed-source implementations and has found several vulnerabilities leading to the publication of two CVEs.
item.author: cs.CR updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-CR 2026] DeepAVR: Deep Analysis via Multi-Agent Collaboration for Automated Vulnerability Repair
item.description: arXiv:2610.32345v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Automated Vulnerability Repair (AVR) has emerged as a critical defense against software security flaws, aiming to triage and fix bugs autonomously. Early LLM-based approaches focused on patch generation under the assumption of perfect fault localization, while recent end-to-end methods attempt to repair vulnerabilities directly from sanitizer logs. However, these methods often fail when the root cause is deeply hidden--either physically distant from the crash site or logically masked by interdependent errors--making the initial report insufficient. We propose DeepAVR, a multi-agent framework for end-to-end AVR that performs deep analysis by transforming intermediate repair outcomes into structured diagnostic feedback. DeepAVR decomposes repair into specialized roles--Fault Localization, Patch Generation, Compile Validation, Security Validation, Functionality Validation, and Patch Review--and routes feedback across these roles to iteratively refine both localization and patch hypotheses. In particular, DeepAVR introduces patch-conditioned re-localization, which treats execution results from intermediate patches as diagnostic signals to uncover hidden root causes, and a root-cause-oriented patch review stage that detects symptom-level fixes and incomplete repairs beyond execution-based validation. Evaluation on the real-world C/C++ vulnerability repair dataset VulnLoc shows that DeepAVR significantly outperforms prior methods, generating correct patches for 92.3% of vulnerabilities. Furthermore, results on SAN2VULN demonstrate strong generalization, with DeepAVR effectively repairing vulnerabilities unseen during training.
item.author: cs.CR updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-CR 2026] Memoir: Learning, Verifying, and Evolving False-Positive Memories for Static Application Security Testing Tools
item.description: arXiv:2608.09181v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Static Application Security Testing (SAST) tools have become indispensable in modern secure software devel- opment. However, these tools often generate false-positive (FP) alerts, imposing substantial manual inspection costs and reducing the trust from developers. Existing FP reduction methods still face two primary challenges. First, the large differences among SAST tools and vulnerability categories make it difficult for these methods to learn recurring patterns in historical false positives. Moreover, the knowledge used by these methods are largely static and cannot be updated as newly validated cases accumulate. To address these challenges, we propose Memoir, a memory- driven framework for identifying false positives by transform- ing historical FP alerts into reusable semantic memories. It consists of two key modules. First, historical semantic memory construction converts historical FP alerts into structured semantic memories through LLM-guided annotation, pattern clustering, and memory synthesis to capture reusable behavioral patterns. Moreover, memory-driven identification and evolution retrieves relevant memories and performs semantic verification against taxonomy consistency and security invariants before making the final prediction. It then incorporates verified predictions back into the memory repository, allowing the knowledge base to evolve as new cases accumulate. We evaluate Memoir on CWE- Bench-Java to demonstrate its effectiveness in real-world security analysis. Specifically, Memoir achieves an F1-score of 99.43% with a Recall of 98.88% and perfect Precision, consistently outperforming other baselines. Furthermore, an industrial case study on production software systems from a top IT company shows that the learned memory base generalizes effectively across different SAST tools without retraining.
item.author: cs.CR updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-SE 2026] Pairing Matters: Performance, Failures, and Efficiency in Lightweight Coding Agents
item.description: arXiv:2610.32131v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Self-hosting coding agents is often necessary for software-engineering teams that must keep proprietary code and development traces within controlled infrastructure. Lightweight, open-weight models make such deployment more feasible by reducing hardware requirements, while strong results on repository-level benchmarks demonstrate their potential for demanding coding tasks. Deploying these models as coding agents requires pairing them with an agent harness, making their joint performance a key deployment consideration. Yet existing leaderboards primarily report fixed harness-model configurations rather than controlled comparisons across alternative pairings. To address this gap, we investigate harness-model interactions through a controlled full-factorial evaluation of six open-source harnesses and three lightweight coding models across 100 SWE-bench Verified tasks, producing 1,800 graded runs under common serving, metering, and grading conditions. For the same model, resolution rates differ by up to 44 percentage points across harnesses, while harness rankings change across models. We apply an evidence-based failure taxonomy to 1,100 unsuccessful runs and find substantial differences in failure patterns across harness-model pairings. A model's dominant failure modes under one harness need not dominate under another. Efficiency is similarly dependent on the pairing: even among model-directed loop harnesses, charged tokens per resolved task vary by more than 20-fold. These findings make harness-model selection a central deployment decision for lightweight coding agents. Strong performance with one harness or model does not guarantee similar results with another. We translate these findings into practitioner guidance for pairing selection, token-efficiency assessment, and trajectory-informed harness engineering, and release the complete experimental records and analysis artifacts.
item.author: cs.SE updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-SE 2026] Large-Scale Study of GitHub Copilot Trajectories
item.description: arXiv:2610.32313v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI coding agents are increasingly integrated into software development workflows. However, most coding agent studies rely on benchmarks similar to SWE-bench, which assume autonomous agents operating in a single trajectory. This assumption does not mirror real-world usage, where developers interactively collaborate with agents. We address this gap by studying human-in-the-loop agent trajectories in the wild, focusing on 7,581 Copilot-authored PRs with publicly accessible session data. We find that 58% of Copilot PRs have no human intervention, and that when developers do intervene, collaboration is brief (median of 2 Human-AI loops). Merged PRs also tend to have fewer initial trajectory iterations than unmerged ones. We also find that the trajectory following the first human intervention exhibits a significant drop of 20.8 iterations and 8.4 min in duration. However, trajectories following later interventions show minimal iteration drops and no significant duration change, signifying that most of the work happens in the initial trajectory. Our qualitative analysis of illustrative PRs explains this pattern: many developer interventions are small, focused requests that Copilot completes in shorter later trajectories. We also illustrate that developers collaborate with Copilot in multiple ways, including delegated work through feedback as well as adding their own commits. However, we find that developers may need to guide Copilot through multiple (sometimes repeated) interventions in the PR, or even across multiple editions of the PR.
item.author: cs.SE updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-SE 2026] From Faulty Claims to Incorrect Patches: An Empirical Study of Task-Grounded Reasoning in Coding Agents
item.description: arXiv:2610.32338v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based coding agents increasingly resolve real-world software engineering tasks, yet still fail on many of them. Prior trajectory studies characterize these failures through task-agnostic patterns of agent behavior, such as repeated actions. However, an agent may follow a sound workflow yet act on a faulty understanding of the existing code, the task requirements, or a candidate fix. Reasoning models, which power most state-of-the-art coding agents, reveal this understanding in their native chain-of-thought (CoT), whose claims about the task can be checked against the facts. Yet it remains unclear how many such checkable claims the CoT contains, how many are faulty, and whether faulty claims actually cause incorrect patches. We present the first empirical study of such claims, which we term task-grounded reasoning, analyzing 400 trajectories of four open-weight reasoning models on SWE-bench Pro. We extract atomic claims from the CoT with an LLM, assess them against evidence gathered by an LLM agent, and manually trace the defects of incorrect patches back to faulty claims, confirming each link with a claim-corrected replay. Task-grounded reasoning covers only 18.5% of the CoT tokens, yet yields 191 atomic claims per trajectory, at least 9.6% of which are faulty. Faulty claims also occur in 96.7% of the resolved trajectories, so their mere presence is a weak signal of failure. Yet two thirds of the 188 incorrect patches trace back to faulty claims. Correcting such a claim makes the agent fix the linked defect in 89.0% of the cases, and correcting all such claims resolves 11.7% of the failed tasks. Our findings show that the CoT carries task-specific signals for diagnosing and repairing agent failures, but exploiting them requires pinpointing the few faulty claims that actually cause patch defects.
item.author: cs.SE updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-SE 2026] OpenDraco: A Platform for Engineering and Experimenting with Configurable Multi-Agent Architectures for Software Engineering
item.description: arXiv:2610.32686v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Experimenting with LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) involves an iterative cycle of modeling configurations, executing and evaluating them, comparing results, and refining system designs. Existing approaches provide limited end-to-end support for this experimentation lifecycle. We present OpenDraco, an open-source platform that integrates these activities into a single workflow. OpenDraco represents agents, prompts, tools, models, parameters, and communication topology in exportable, versioned JSON specifications, translated into executable LangGraph workflows supporting different interaction structures. Users can modify and re-evaluate configurations using local or cloud-based LLMs. We instantiate OpenDraco for automated program repair (APR) and evaluate a sequential baseline and seven reconstructed configurations on synthetic and real-world SWE-bench Lite issues. The results reveal substantial cost differences among configurations with similar repair outcomes, while the baseline resolves 12 of 77 SWE-bench issues using open-source LLMs. Additional proof-of-concept tasks illustrate applicability beyond APR. OpenDraco supports iterative experimentation with heterogeneous MAS configurations, enabling researchers to examine their outcomes and costs within a common environment. Demonstration video: https://youtu.be/278sOR4lBEk.
item.author: cs.SE updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-SE 2026] Loop Engineering: Building Blocks, Adoption, and Impact
item.description: arXiv:2608.21884v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Over the past months, the way developers guide agentic AI coding tools has moved up several levels of abstraction, from phrasing prompts to engineering context to configuring the harness around the underlying model. In June 2026, practitioners began to describe a new level called loop engineering: Instead of prompting an agent interactively, developers design systems that prompt agents for them. The term spread rapidly, accompanied by bold claims and vocal skepticism, but its adoption in software projects has not yet been measured. We present (1) an exploratory review of the emerging gray literature on loop engineering, (2) a traceability analysis and an exploratory mining study of 36,710 software repositories, and (3) the design of a controlled experiment to study how loop goals, static analysis checks, and decision policies affect task success, code quality, resource usage, and token consumption of agent loops. Our literature review found broad agreement on what a well-engineered loop contains: agent loops started on a schedule or by repository events and bounded by machine-checkable stop conditions, persistent state files, verifier subagents, token budgets, and defined points of escalation to humans. These sources provide no systematic evidence of the claimed benefits. In the mining study, we found autonomous agent loops in 217 open-source GitHub repositories using heuristics and behavioral signals. Nearly all of these repositories committed the configuration that starts their loops, but almost none of them committed the state files that the gray literature suggests. Our proposed experiment is a first step toward closing the evidence gap identified in our literature review. We call for further empirical studies of the benefits and costs of loop engineering for software engineering tasks.
item.author: cs.SE updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-CL 2026] VEILED-SH: Vulnerability Expression through Indirect Language Evaluation Dataset (Self-Harm)
item.description: arXiv:2610.26190v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: AI systems may miss indirect, culturally situated distress or provide support mismatched to the application context. Existing benchmarks do not jointly address cultural variation, application context, and practitioner disagreement. We introduce VEILED-SH, a benchmark and construction methodology for evaluating single-turn responses to indirect expressions of suicide, self-harm, and distress. Its 10,003 prompts span counselor chat, forum posts, platform search, and triage, drawing on Singapore-grounded sources and public datasets. An expert-validated multi-label taxonomy distinguishes intent, communicative function, and response behavior. Six automated profiles, individually calibrated to three peer-support practitioners and three clinicians, retain separate reference policies for proxy-alignment scoring. Evaluating five systems on a coverage-enriched sample reveals variation in proxy alignment across profile-generated reference policies, even for the same system responses.
item.author: cs.CL updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-SE 2026] Code Comprehensor: Hierarchical Documentation and Cross-Modal Retrieval for Large Repositories
item.description: arXiv:2610.30016v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Understanding large, complex, and rapidly evolving code bases remains a core challenge for software engineering at scale, hindering onboarding, maintenance, refactoring, and impact analysis. Providing this information to a Large-Language Model (LLM) is another hurdle, as the LLM must understand not only the required code method but also its associated methods in the grand scheme of the repository. We propose Code Comprehensor, a hybrid retrieval-reasoning framework combining (i) CodeGraph, a code dependency callgraph, (ii) CodeScribe, which uses code-aware LLMs to generate hierarchical documentation across repository call graphs, and (iii) CodeContrast, a CLIP-style dual-encoder model trained on CodeScribe output to learn aligned text-code embeddings. CodeContrast enables fast, semantically precise retrieval of relevant code-context neighborhoods, which serve as grounded evidence for an MCP-based LLM orchestrator answering domain-specific queries. Evaluation on OpenCV and a proprietary 5M-LOC repository shows that CodeScribe-derived supervision significantly improves cross-modal retrieval in text-to-code accuracy over baseline approaches. Richer textual supervision (hierarchical documentation, parent/sibling context, and LLM-generated synthetic questions) consistently enhances performance across both repositories. LLM-as-a-judge evaluation using the popular RAGAS of the Code Comprehensor output yields above 90% faithfulness scores.

item.title: [arXiv-CR 2026] DEFEAT: Stitching Fragmented File I/O Contexts for Early Ransomware Detection
item.description: arXiv:2609.21426v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Ransomware increasingly fragments its file operations across temporary and intermediate files, scattering the semantic context that links individual I/O events to an overarching encryption campaign. This fragmentation defeats existing detectors that reason over isolated file streams -- whether pattern-based methods that match rigid event sequences or learning-based methods that require accumulating statistical evidence across many files. We present DEFEAT, a framework that reconstructs this fragmented, scattered context by grouping causally related file events into File Event Gadgets (FEGs), semantically coherent units that capture the full intent behind sequences of file operations spanning multiple dynamically created files. Unlike provenance graphs (system-wide causal graphs that record relationships among all OS entities, such as processes, files, sockets, and registry keys, across the entire system), FEGs are scoped to the file-operation context of a single user asset, enabling lightweight, targeted analysis without whole-system instrumentation. Each FEG is modelled as an attributed control flow graph (ACFG) and embedded via a graph neural network for unsupervised clustering, enabling analysts to label entire behavioural clusters rather than individual samples, reducing annotation effort by 94%. Evaluated on a corpus of 97,816,471 file I/O events spanning 67 ransomware families, DEFEAT achieves 99.2% detection accuracy and outperforms state-of-the-art methods including UNVEIL, RWGuard, and Peeler by 6.57 to 7.56%. The framework operates at the granularity of a single file encryption: because each ACFG represents exactly one FEG (one user asset context), a cluster label can be assigned as soon as the first file operation completes, enabling detection at the first encrypted file.

item.title: [arXiv-CR 2026] Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling
item.description: arXiv:2610.30184v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Security bugs often slip past static analysis not because they are impossible to detect, but because detection rules have not yet been written for the code in front of us. New frameworks, APIs, and coding idioms continually create such gaps, leaving developers to discover failures and manually encode new rules. We present SESAA, a framework in which an Large Language Model (LLM) agent starts from no rules and iteratively evolves a set of readable and auditable joern queries. The agent receives feedback only from a second LLM critic, which inspects flagged and unflagged code to identify likely false alarms and suspected misses, without access to ground-truth labels. The agent then uses this feedback to revise its queries. On the OWASP Benchmark for Python, SESAA reaches a mean F1 of 0.742 across 8 independent runs, well above the default configurations of five widely used tools and comparable to the strongest of them once it is tuned with access to ground-truth labels that SESAA never sees. In a pilot on real-world Python projects, queries induced from code available before a vulnerability was introduced detect 10 of 19 subsequent CVEs, including 9 detected by rules written for the same repository. The resulting detector is a set of executable, human-readable queries that engineers can inspect, modify, and run independently. These results suggest that LLM agents can turn static-analysis rule maintenance from a manually authored process into an iterative process of automated discovery and repair.
item.author: cs.CR updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-CR 2026] JANUS: Agentic Cross-Language Fuzzing Harness Generation for Android Native Libraries
item.description: arXiv:2610.30218v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Modern Android apps extensively rely on native libraries, bridging Java/Kotlin and C/C++ through the Java Native Interface (JNI). This cross-language interoperation, however, exposes the memory-safe Android Runtime to the unsafe C/C++ world, creating an attack surface that has been repeatedly exploited for full device compromise. While fuzzing is a proven technique for vetting native libraries, state-of-the-art harness generation tools struggle to faithfully capture closed-source cross-language API usage: (i) precise program analysis across the JNI boundary does not scale, whereas lightweight approximations miss critical invocation patterns; and (ii) none tackles the construction of complex composite objects consumed by JNI methods. In this paper, we propose JANUS, the first agentic approach to synthesizing cross-language JNI-aware fuzzing harnesses for Android native libraries. JANUS iteratively resolves both explicit and implicit cross-language call dependencies to recover app-specific runtime context, and recursively assembles cross-language argument objects in a bottom-up manner. JANUS leverages an autonomous agentic workflow to reduce reliance on hand-crafted heuristics, capturing the vast landscape of hidden API usage knowledge embedded in closed-source native libraries. Evaluation on 44 popular real-world apps (such as Google and YouTube Music, covering 21,386 JNI methods total) shows that JANUS produces over 5.9 times as many valid harnesses (6,094) as state-of-the-art automatic harnessing tools. On pre-installed apps from five mainstream Android vendors (e.g., Xiaomi, Vivo, Samsung), JANUS further uncovers 6 previously unknown vulnerabilities in closed-source native libraries.

item.title: [arXiv-SE 2026] Beyond Accuracy: Disentangling Decomposition from Typed-State Quality Assurance in Multi-Agent LLM Pipelines
item.description: arXiv:2610.31280v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-agent LLM pipelines are often credited with gains in software engineering tasks, but it is rarely clear whether a gain stems from the typed contract between agents or from the specialized prompts that decomposition enables. We study this attribution problem in Requirements Engineering, comparing three architectures for classifying requirements as functional or non-functional and then prioritizing them with MoSCoW: a single-call baseline; a two-call variant that reuses the pipeline's specialized prompts but passes an unvalidated intermediate; and a pipeline with a Pydantic-validated typed state. The 18 conditions cover PROMISE NFR+ (625 requirements), three locally hosted small language models, and two languages. The F1 gain over the baseline is associated with the two-call, specialized-prompt variant (up to +0.075), whereas the typed state adds a small difference (-0.003 to +0.013) that is significant in one of six comparisons. Beyond accuracy, the typed pipeline contains out-of-range model outputs at the agent boundary, while the unvalidated variant fails later and drops the requirement, and it shows a small, reproducible increase in inter-model MoSCoW consistency whose cause our design cannot isolate. The study is associative: the contrasts bundle prompts, call count, and staged context, and the results come from three 7--8B models on one dataset. The implementation and replication package are archived on Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23380444).
item.author: cs.SE updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-SE 2026] Typed Template Fuzzing
item.description: arXiv:2610.31342v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fuzzing software with complex inputs has been a longstanding challenge. Traditionally, fuzzers either programmatically encode language constraints, requiring significant engineering effort, or rely on users to declare grammars and constraints. Recent LLM-based fuzzers address these drawbacks but introduce new issues. Some use LLMs for test generation, sacrificing throughput and producing invalid inputs when the LLM makes mistakes. Others rely on language-specific parsers, static analysis, and AST manipulation libraries. We introduce Typed Template Fuzzing (TTF), a lightweight LLM-based fuzzing methodology. The key idea is to use LLMs in a preprocessing step to transform seeds into typed templates. The typed templates then enable semantically aware, mutation-based fuzzing without language-specific parsers, type checkers, or further LLM queries during fuzzing. By exploiting the correspondence between seeds and templates, TTF can moreover repair LLM mistakes. We have implemented TTF in our tool Typos, which we evaluate across 21 input languages, including C, C++, Go, Rust, SystemVerilog, Scala, and Java, as well as libraries such as PyTorch and Qiskit. In a six-month fuzzing campaign, we reported 135 bugs, 128 of which were previously unknown. Perhaps most notably, on average 96% of Typos's mutants are valid, coming close to the validity rates of domain-specific fuzzers. Our evaluation further shows Typos's benefits over the state of the art.
item.author: cs.SE updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-AI 2026] RIPPLE: Recovery Internalization through Process-Level Policy Learning and Effect-Aware Credit for Long-Horizon Agentic Coding
item.description: arXiv:2610.31276v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-horizon coding agents can observe a failure and generate a plausible critique yet continue along the same incorrect trajectory. We call this the Critique-to-Action Handoff Gap. We introduce RIPPLE, a recovery-oriented training framework that internalizes process-level guidance into a single self-recovering policy. A prefix-only teacher provides evidence-grounded recovery supervision without access to future actions or terminal outcomes. After lightweight distillation, reinforcement learning assigns stage-specific credit to reflection triggering, diagnosis, and corrective action. Local validity signals gate trajectory advantages so that intermediate recovery decisions do not indiscriminately inherit terminal outcomes. Across four repository-level software-engineering benchmarks, RIPPLE improves the base policy by an arithmetic mean of 4.8 score points, with no auxiliary critic at deployment. Controlled ablations isolate the benefits of local, stage-aligned credit, and matched-prefix interventions show that critique semantics affect subsequent correction. Recovery gains concentrate where the prefix contains sufficient diagnostic evidence and the repository state remains reversible within the remaining budget.
item.author: cs.AI updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-SE 2026] WEAVE: Weaving Real-World Code Evolution into Dependency-Structured Tasks for Benchmarking and Training Code Agents
item.description: arXiv:2610.22039v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Real-world software engineering rarely consists of isolated changes. Features, migrations, and systematic fixes often unfold across multiple pull requests (PRs), requiring coordinated modifications across a repository. Yet most executable repository-level benchmarks retain a single issue or PR as the task unit, while existing multi-PR settings rely on coarse aggregation and structure-agnostic evaluation. This mismatch obscures dependencies among changes and limits progress measurement and learning signals for long-horizon code agents. We introduce WEAVE, a framework that transforms verified PR histories into executable, dependency-structured tasks. WEAVE leverages repository-calibrated typed change loci to organize related PRs into bounded DAGs and instantiate each as a unified executable task. We further introduce Graph Credit, a deterministic, test-grounded metric that measures dependency-consistent partial progress and supports dense, verifiable rewards for reinforcement learning. Experiments on task construction, agent evaluation, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning show that WEAVE yields coherent executable tasks, enables more faithful progress measurement than flat scoring, and provides effective supervision and verifiable rewards for training code agents.
item.author: cs.SE updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-AI 2026] SkillNEO: Non-Elitist Evolutionary Optimization of Agent Skills
item.description: arXiv:2610.20926v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Agent skills turn procedural knowledge into reusable artifacts, allowing LLM agents to accumulate and refine expertise through experience. Building on this, skill evolution iteratively improves skills using execution feedback. However, improvement may require several interdependent edits, so low-reward versions can still be worth developing. Requiring immediate reward gains can discard useful partial repairs before their benefits emerge. Non-elitist evolution allows new versions to receive further edits despite scoring below earlier ones. For agent skills, this calls for evidence of what to preserve and repair next. We introduce SkillNEO (Non-Elitist Evolutionary Optimization for Agent Skills), which separately selects a version to use and versions to keep improving. Comparing how related versions perform the same task reveals working steps to preserve and remaining failures to fix. It can also revisit and revise earlier versions using later evidence. Across 86 SkillsBench tasks in eight domains, including software engineering and office work, SkillNEO raises GPT-5.4 Mini's average reward from 49.1% to 66.4%, within GPT-5.5 and GPT-5.6 Luna's original-skill range. Mini executes tasks, proposes revisions, and edits skills; final evaluation uses the same task instances. Gains span all eight domains. The same skills improve stronger models without further editing. On the 41 tasks with modified skills, reuse improves Luna by 10.5 percentage points and places GPT-5.5 10.6 points above its published original-skill reference. Execution records show these skills can benefit stronger models even when Mini still fails some task requirements. Search histories also show lower-scoring versions leading to skills ultimately selected for use. Together, these findings show that skill evolution can turn a weaker model's partial progress into reusable procedural knowledge for improving more capable agents.
item.author: cs.AI updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-CL 2026] OPRD: On-Policy Reminder Distillation for Long-Horizon Coding Agents
item.description: arXiv:2610.21496v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reliable repository-level coding requires agents not only to generate correct code but also to preserve constraints and respond to tool feedback across long interactions. However, our diagnostic analysis shows that agents often fail to act on relevant information already available in context, while final Pass/Fail outcomes provide only sparse process supervision. We introduce On-Policy Reminder Distillation (OPRD), which combines Multi-Scope Reminder supervision with outcome-based routing on reminder-free student rollouts. Successful rollouts provide autoregressive self-imitation targets, whereas failed rollouts receive Reminder-conditioned reverse-KL supervision from a teacher that re-evaluates the same student-generated prefixes. A Global Reminder converts final-test diagnostics into trajectory-level guidance, while Turn-local Reminders apply only to the next decision following the relevant environment observation. The teacher and student share a two-stage initialization from Coding SFT and Instruction-Following (IF) SFT. At inference, the student operates without Reminders. On SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Pro, and SWE-bench Multilingual, OPRD improves the benchmark-averaged task resolution rate by 11.3 points over the open-source Qwen3.5-4B base model. Under the same diagnostic protocol, it reduces the aggregate error-event count from 446 to 222, a 50.2% reduction.
item.author: cs.CL updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-CR 2026] PatchRisk: Forecasting Future Vulnerability Exposure in Open-Source Dependency Networks
item.description: arXiv:2609.13719v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Open-source software ecosystems are web-scale dependency networks. A downstream package can become exposed to security risk not because its own source code changes, but because one of its transitive dependencies later receives a vulnerability advisory. Existing vulnerability-detection work often focuses on whether code is currently vulnerable or whether a known vulnerable dependency is already present. We study a different problem: future transitive vulnerability exposure. Given a package-version dependency graph observed at release time, the task is to predict whether any non-root dependency will receive a vulnerability advisory within a future horizon. This problem is important for Web intelligence and software supply-chain security because it supports proactive dependency triage before future exposure is visible. It is also easy to evaluate incorrectly: current vulnerable dependencies can leak the label, and different versions of the same root package can create package-level memorization across train and test splits. We therefore construct PatchRisk, a leakage-aware benchmark from Open Source Vulnerability advisories and deps.dev dependency graphs for npm and PyPI. The benchmark uses filtration-aware labels, package-disjoint evaluation, temporal testing, and nested 1K, 3K, 5K, and 10K sampling scales. The largest cleaned setting contains 9,007 root package-version graphs spanning 4,157 root packages. We evaluate three feature families: TimeOnly, GraphStruct, and HistoryGraph. On the 10K temporal-test benchmark, HistoryGraph improves AUPRC over the strongest TimeOnly baseline from 0.351 to 0.640 for 90-day forecasting and from 0.473 to 0.813 for 365-day forecasting. The improvement remains stable across smaller scales and package-group shuffle robustness tests.
item.author: cs.CR updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-SE 2026] Learning from Repair Experience: Self-Evolving Agents for Automated Vulnerability Repair
item.description: arXiv:2605.30105v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promise for automated vulnerability repair (AVR), but they still face several limitations, including the lack of intra-vulnerability experience accumulation and the lack of cross-vulnerability experience reuse. As a result, LLMs may repeatedly make similar mistakes during iterative repair and underutilize valuable repair knowledge from historical vulnerabilities. To address these challenges, we propose EvoRepair, an experience-based self-evolving AVR agent framework that enables LLMs to accumulate, refine, and leverage domain-specific knowledge across long-horizon vulnerability repairs. EvoRepair follows a cyclic learn-and-repair process that retrieves relevant past experiences to guide repair, extracts new experiences from repair trajectories, and updates an experience bank using quality-aware scoring. We evaluate EvoRepair against 15 representative vulnerability repair baselines on PATCHEVAL and SEC-bench. Results show that EvoRepair achieves the best overall performance, reaching 93.47% on PATCHEVAL, 87.00% on SEC-bench, and 90.46% overall. In particular, EvoRepair outperforms the latest LLM-based baseline LoopRepair by 39.56% and 33.50% on PATCHEVAL and SEC-bench, respectively, and surpasses IntentFix by 70.86% and 50.50%. Across both benchmarks, EvoRepair also exceeds the recent self-evolving agent Live-SWE-Agent by 6.98% overall. Additional transfer experiments on VUL4J further demonstrate the robustness of EvoRepair across models, programming languages, and datasets. These findings demonstrate that experience-based self-evolution substantially strengthens agentic AVR and goes beyond existing self-evolving techniques.
item.author: cs.SE updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-CR 2026] How Much Does the Harness Matter, and for Whom? A Multi-Model Study of Context in LLM-Driven Vulnerability Discovery
item.description: arXiv:2610.28802v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How much does an agent harness affect vulnerability discovery, and does its value depend on the model? We study 24 model-runner configurations using an open-source harness on a production codebase whose vulnerabilities were non-public at scan time. The pipeline combines static screening, LLM investigation, model self-revalidation, root-cause mapping, independent source review, and isolated proof-of-concept confirmation. Across 265 confirmed security root causes, the largest two-run configuration covers 60.4%, while 14.3% are found by exactly one model. No single configuration covers all observed findings. In a four-model context experiment, moving from a minimal prompt to an engineered prompt with a CodeQL-derived call graph raises criticality-weighted yield by 20-86% for smaller and mid-tier models, compared with 2% for the frontier model. This comparison changes both prompt and context. Separating those effects shows that the engineered prompt improves yield for all four models, while adding CodeQL context beyond that prompt improves yield only for the smallest model. A held-out CyberGym subset shows the same direction of target-recall improvement for the combined treatment. Frontier models achieve low false-report rates but do not consistently achieve the highest yield. Strong lower-cost models can deliver similar performance at an order of magnitude lower cost. These results support matching models, prompts, and context to the task, and combining configurations for broader coverage.
item.author: cs.CR updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-CR 2026] Where AI Vulnerability Discovery Harnesses Go Quiet: Structural False Negatives and Hidden Vulnerabilities
item.description: arXiv:2610.29379v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM-based vulnerability discovery harnesses can miss real, reachable vulnerabilities because of how the harness around the model is built. Steps that select code, filter it, and store and merge findings can drop a vulnerability before or after the model runs, independently of the model's capability, and the report usually gives no sign that this happened. These drops come from engineering choices, and errors. They leave vulnerabilities undetected, and an attacker who knows the harness's rules can also use them to hide a vulnerability on purpose. Understanding these drops shows how to build harnesses that fix or disclose them and are harder to evade. Starting from the two harnesses we maintain, Knostic's OpenAnt and raptor, and then examining 10 additional open-source harnesses, we mapped 13 points where such drops occur and organized them into a taxonomy. Using each harness's own code, we show a single file that six harnesses dropped before their model saw its code, five of them without notice. We propose engineering failure patterns mapped to these drops, and relate them to Ptacek and Newsham's work on intrusion detection evasion. The paper also covers content-steered verdicts and prompt injection, and gives design principles and tests for harnesses that report accurately what they analyzed. The reliability findings likely apply to other LLM harnesses, beyond vulnerability research and application security, and the evasion findings apply wherever an attacker can write or influence the code being checked. We also argue that harnesses built to be descriptive can, in effect, be prescriptive. Rules written to describe typical code and typical model replies end up deciding what is analyzed, and anything that does not conform is treated as absent or as "no vulnerability."
item.author: cs.CR updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-CR 2026] CertMoE: Robustness Certification for Mixture-of-Experts LLMs via Routing-Aware Smoothing
item.description: arXiv:2610.29395v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Provable robustness is a cornerstone of trustworthy machine learning, aiming to guarantee model predictions under adversarial perturbations. Existing certification frameworks, inspired by abstract interpretation or symbolic execution, typically assume a fixed computation graph, where input perturbations or variations affect only model outputs but not the underlying execution path. This assumption, however, is violated in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Large Language Models (LLMs), whose input-dependent routing induces discrete and dynamic execution paths. Crucially, this dynamic computation changes the certified object from a single fixed function to a composition of input-dependent sub-functions, leading to unreliable certification guarantees. This paper presents \textsc{CertMoE}, the first routing-aware robustness certification framework for MoE LLMs, which explicitly accounts for input-induced routing dynamics in certification. Specifically, we introduce a relaxed routing-containment criterion, which certifies that perturbed Top-$K$ routing is contained within a larger certified expert pool. Based on this guarantee, \textsc{CertMoE} then constructs the corresponding induced sub-network and certifies its prediction consistency. This hierarchical certification procedure yields a joint probabilistic guarantee over routing containment and sub-network robustness, providing sufficient conditions under which the original prediction remains invariant. Extensive experiments across recent MoE LLMs demonstrate that dynamic routing makes certificates issued by existing methods frequently violated, while \textsc{CertMoE} reduces the empirical violation rate with routing-aware guarantees, e.g., from more than $30\%$ to $0$, yielding certificates that more faithfully reflect the robustness of MoE models.
item.author: cs.CR updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-SE 2026] Where Should a Stuck Agent Spend Its Next Tokens? Causal Attribution of Inference-Time Resources
item.description: arXiv:2610.28834v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Inference-time scaling is often treated as a token-budget problem, but a failed coding agent can seek qualitatively different resources: computation, information, or feedback. We introduce Banzhaf Resource Attribution (BRA), a controlled factorial framework that measures each resource's marginal contribution to repair and its interactions while holding the failed state and revision protocol fixed. We evaluate six models on 194 function-level failures from MBPP+ and HumanEval+ and 126 repository-level failures from SWE-bench Verified. Task-relevant specifications consistently improve repair, whereas public-test feedback provides small gains and retrieved code little to none. The value of additional computation declines with model capability, while information remains useful; resource channels largely exhibit diminishing returns, although complementary information can reinforce itself. Yet three of four frontier models select feedback in 95-100% of cases and obtain lower gains than uniform random resource selection. BRA thus exposes a gap between the resources agents prefer and those that measurably improve repair.

item.title: [arXiv-SE 2026] RegoMender: A Multi-agent Framework for Automated Rego Policy Repair
item.description: arXiv:2610.29456v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Policy-as-Code (PaC) has emerged as a foundational paradigm in cloud-native systems. However, repairing Rego policies remains challenging due to their strict syntax, declarative semantics, and specific verification requirements. Existing automated program repair (APR) methods are mainly designed for mainstream languages and struggle to accommodate the unique policy logic and repair workflows of Rego. Thus, Rego policy repair remains a manual process driven by trial and error. To address this, we introduce RegoBench, the first automated Rego policy benchmark comprising 1,159 real-world defects, and propose RegoMender, a feedback-guided multi-agent framework. Collaborating via a shared blackboard and an atomic toolkit, RegoMender dynamically executes patching, rewriting, or rolling back, to resolve complex repair scenarios. Evaluated on RegoBench, RegoMender achieves syntactic and test-based semantic success rates of 82.9\% and 77.9\%, respectively, outperforming the strongest baseline by 13.4\%. Unlike other approaches whose performance drops in complex scenarios, RegoMender maintains effectiveness across single-step and chained repair tasks. Furthermore, it generalizes strongly across HCL and SQL and achieves an 86.4\% repair rate on 132 real-world CVE vulnerabilities, proving its robustness and practical utility for security.
item.author: cs.SE updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-SE 2026] Benchmarking Coding Agents for System-Level Performance Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2610.29695v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coding agents are becoming an increasingly important paradigm for automating software engineering tasks. However, existing coding benchmarks primarily evaluate agents at the function or repository level, leaving their capabilities in more complex distributed software systems largely unexplored. In practice, many modern applications adopt microservice architectures, where end-to-end performance emerges from interactions among multiple independently running services, requiring agents to reason beyond local code changes. To study this capability, we introduce MicroPerf-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating coding agents on end-to-end performance optimization in microservice systems. Constructing such a benchmark is challenging because reproducible system-level performance fixes are sparse and difficult to attribute. We address this challenge by injecting empirically grounded performance anti-patterns into real-world open-source systems while preserving functionality and ensuring measurable performance degradation. The resulting benchmark contains 65 optimization instances across seven systems and nine anti-patterns, each with an executable environment, functional tests, and mixed-workload evaluation. Across 1,755 runs covering nine agent-model configurations, the best configuration recovers only 42.0% of the injected performance degradation. The dominant failure is not invalid code, but functionally correct and constraint-compliant changes that fail to improve end-to-end performance, highlighting system-level bottleneck localization as a key challenge for current coding agents. The source code and data are available at https://github.com/zyzcjnb/microperf.
item.author: cs.SE updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-SE 2026] Metamodel-Guided LLM Decoding for Consistent DSL Generation
item.description: arXiv:2610.29749v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate software engineering artifacts written in domain-specific languages (DSLs). Correct DSL instances usually must comply with not only the concrete syntax but also the abstract syntax defined by a metamodel augmented with semantic well-formedness constraints. Existing constrained decoding approaches typically guarantee compliance only with concrete syntax or with a limited set of semantic constraints expressed over the generated text, making metamodel-level constraint consistency difficult to enforce during generation. We present MeMoDecode: a decoding framework that enforces a DSL's concrete syntax, abstract syntax, and well-formedness constraints jointly. Specifically, whenever the LLM generates a complete metamodel concept, MeMoDecode incrementally maps the current output to a partial model and verifies whether it can still be completed into a consistent instance. We combine MeMoDecode with a simple retry mechanism that resumes decoding from the most recent completable snapshot whenever an inconsistency is detected. Under a sound backend verifier, MeMoDecode never performs worse than grammar-constrained decoding on alignment metrics satisfying natural assumptions. Across four DSLs and six open-weight LLMs ranging from 0.6B to 70B parameters, MeMoDecode achieves the highest consistency, improving consistency by 23% on average over unconstrained decoding and by 8% on average over grammar-constrained decoding. It also improves benchmark performance while incurring only modest runtime overhead. These results show that metamodel-guided decoding is an effective approach for enforcing DSL consistency during decoding across diverse DSLs and LLM scales.
item.author: cs.SE updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-SE 2026] AssureCode: Structured Justification for Trustworthy Agentic Coding
item.description: arXiv:2610.29758v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The use of AI-based tools in software development is rapidly changing how software is produced, enabling large volumes of code to be generated with limited human implementation effort. However, this raises fundamental challenges for ensuring that generated artifacts are aligned with developer intent and have been appropriately validated. In this work, we propose the use of structured argumentation in driving AI-assisted software development. Inspired by techniques from assurance engineering for safety-critical systems, we define a language of justification rationales that explicitly relate informal natural language prompts, formal specifications, assumptions about developer intentions, and program analysis evidence in a structured and verifiable format. We then describe AssureCode, a tool-supported methodology for creating such rationales as part of agentic code generation. We provide an empirical analysis of our implementation where we investigate its capacity to contribute towards justified assurance of correctness for AI-generated code.
item.author: cs.SE updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-SE 2026] PAUSE: Search-Free Steering of Coding Agents Before Their First Source-Code Edit
item.description: arXiv:2610.29870v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coding agents can invest substantial effort in repository exploration and testing yet still produce unsuccessful patches. Existing online steering methods review trajectories periodically or invoke an advisor when a monitor detects behavioral problems; frequent reviews are costly, and the absence of anomalous behavior does not mean that an agent is on the right track. We propose PAUSE, a framework for steering coding agents with a single planning intervention. Agents reach their first source-code edit at a median of 60% of trajectory progress, after exploration, bug reproduction, and testing. PAUSE intercepts this edit request before it executes, which requires no learned monitor, no search over checkpoints, and no extra model call (search-free). A separate Planner reads the task and the pre-edit transcript and writes one repair plan; the same agent, the Executor, resumes with this plan, keeping its context and workspace. PAUSE applies online, during a live run, and offline, from a recorded trajectory prefix. We evaluate PAUSE on SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench Multilingual with two Executors and three agent harnesses. With Qwen3-coder as Executor and GPT-5.6 Sol as Planner, online steering improves resolution by 16.8% on Verified in OpenHands and by 14.7% on Multilingual in SWE-agent. In SWE-agent, PAUSE outperforms LivePlan, a rule-triggered advisor, by 3.2% on Verified and 3.7% on Multilingual at similar Planner cost, and is comparable to SICA's periodic overseer at about 11-15% of its Planner cost. Offline, PAUSE recovers 35.4% of eligible failed Verified tasks, and resuming from the recorded prefix uses 33-41% fewer Executor tokens than restarting.
item.author: cs.SE updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-SE 2026] SWE-DIVE: Multi-Turn Coding Agent Evaluation with Dynamic User Simulation
item.description: arXiv:2610.30047v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coding agents are typically evaluated using one-shot, well-formulated prompts. Benchmarks such as SWE-bench use existing GitHub issues as input for a coding agent and evaluate whether the agent successfully solves the task. However, in real-world use cases, prompts are often not as well-formulated or structured as existing GitHub issues. Additionally, a coding agent session is not limited to a single prompt; it typically involves a multi-turn interaction in which the user iteratively adds new tasks and requirements that the agent must fulfill. To benchmark these abilities, we developed SWE-DIVE, a dynamic, interactive validation and evaluation framework for benchmarking coding agents in a multi-turn environment. To achieve this, we introduce a user simulator that can simulate different behavioral patterns and communicate with the coding agent. We also introduce a conversation validator that evaluates the user simulator's outputs to determine whether they fulfill the initial requirements and guide the agent toward successfully solving the task. The entire framework is embedded in a Harbor environment, which orchestrates the coding agent, user simulator, and conversation validator, and executes the test environment to determine whether the agent successfully solves the task. Our results and source code are available in our GitHub repository (https://github.com/lorenzbrehme/swe-dive_usersim).

item.title: [arXiv-SE 2026] Generating Mitigations for Downstream Projects to Neutralize Upstream Library Vulnerability
item.description: arXiv:2503.24273v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Third-party libraries are essential in software development as they prevent the need for developers to recreate existing functionalities. However, vulnerabilities within these libraries pose significant risks to dependent projects. Upgrading dependencies is infeasible when no patched version is available or when downstream projects have strict version constraints. Moreover, repairing the vulnerability proves challenging when the source code of the library is inaccessible. State-of-the-art automatic vulnerability repair and automatic program repair methods both fail to address this issue. Therefore, mitigating library vulnerabilities without access to source code or available patches is crucial for a swift response to potential security attacks. Existing tools encounter challenges concerning generalizability and functional security. Upon vulnerability disclosure, LUMEN prepares a pool of candidate mitigation strategies by retrieving explicit workarounds from public sources and supplementing the pool with generated strategies based on vulnerability reproduction behavior. LUMEN then selects a suitable strategy, autonomously gathers repository-specific context, and adaptively generates a validated mitigation patch. We evaluate LUMEN on 474 impacted functions associated with 94 vulnerabilities. LUMEN successfully mitigates 393 functions, achieving a success rate of 82.91%, which substantially outperforms the adapted baseline in blocking vulnerability reproduction under our exploit-based evaluation. Additionally, our ablation study evaluates the contributions of strategy composition, strategy selection, and repository-level context collection. Further evaluations show that LUMEN can mitigate vulnerabilities disclosed after the knowledge cutoff of the base model.
item.author: cs.SE updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [arXiv-SE 2026] MockingBird: Context-aware Repository-level Code Translation with Isolated Validation
item.description: arXiv:2511.21878v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Despite advances in repository-level code translation, automated type resolution across differing type systems and translation validation (functional-equivalence checking) remain challenging. This paper proposes MockingBird, combining context-aware type resolution with mock-based isolated validation. MockingBird retrieves API documentation and contextual code information per source-language type, prompting an LLM to resolve precise cross-language type mappings, reducing the manual effort of existing approaches. Using this automatically constructed type map, MockingBird employs custom serialization/deserialization to generate equivalent target-language mock objects, validating each translation unit in isolation without test translation, eliminating test-overfitting risks and translation challenges. On 10 Java-to-Python tasks from the AlphaTrans benchmark, MockingBird improves functional equivalence from the state-of-the-art 25.14% to 43.10%, with no manual type-mapping correction needed. A 700-fragment study shows MockingBird achieves 0 false positives and 0.9% false negatives, substantially outperforming GraalVM (2.4% false positives, 7.6% false negatives) and MatchFixAgent (11.0% combined mislabel rate). The pipeline is also LLM-agnostic, maintaining these gains with both DeepSeekCoder-33B and the smaller Devstral-24B.
